summary: This specification extends the TLV definitions used by OLSRv2 and the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol so they can accommodate future protocol extensions. It updates RFC 7181 and RFC 6130.

eli5.summary: The message forms had little room for new ideas. This reworks them so future additions fit in.

questions: what is a tlv in manet routing
how should unknown tlv values be handled
subtitle: Rules that let OLSRv2 and NHDP routers shrug off unfamiliar TLV values, so the protocols can be extended safely.

tldr.problem: NHDP and OLSRv2 let an implementation reject a message as badly formed if a TLV carried a value it did not recognize. That makes it hard to add extensions that still work with older, unextended routers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7188 forbids rejecting a message for an unrecognized TLV value, says how to treat TLV values that are longer or shorter than expected, turns the MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE values into bit fields, and creates IANA registries for the TLV values.
tldr.outcome: Older routers now ignore what they do not understand instead of dropping the whole message, and new TLV values can be registered. The RFC updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 and has itself been updated by RFC 7722.

today: RFC 7188 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7722. It updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181.

sections.title: Why the TLV Rules Needed a Fix
sections.content:
The MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP, RFC 6130) and the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2, RFC 7181) are protocols for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). Both are built on the Generalized MANET Packet/Message Format (RFC 5444), which carries information in TLV (Type-Length-Value) elements.

Both base specifications allow an implementation to treat a message as "badly formed" for reasons beyond those they list, and so to reject it. That could be read as allowing rejection of a message just because a TLV value was unrecognized. This document removes that latitude, which gives extensions more room and lets them interoperate with unextended implementations.

TLVs with an unknown type or type extension were already required to be ignored, and are not a reason to reject a message.
sections.eli5: Some old rules said a router could throw away a whole message if it saw something unfamiliar. That made it risky to invent new things, so the rules were changed.

sections.title: Never Reject for an Unrecognized Value
sections.content:
The central rule is that an implementation MUST NOT reject a message because it contains an unrecognized TLV value. An unextended implementation of NHDP or OLSRv2 must instead process or ignore that value as described in the later sections. As a result, the 7th, 10th and 11th bullets in Section 12.1 of RFC 6130 are removed.

The RFC stresses that this is not otherwise a change to the base specifications. Those specifications are written in terms such as "if an address is associated with a value of LOST by a LINK_STATUS TLV". Association with an unrecognized value has no effect on an implementation that strictly follows them.

Unknown TLV types and type extensions were already to be ignored. This rule extends the same tolerance to unknown values of known TLVs.
sections.eli5: If a kid reads a note and finds a word they do not know, they keep reading instead of crumpling it up. The rest of the note is still useful.

sections.title: Handling Unexpected TLV Value Lengths
sections.content:
A TLV can hold one value or several (a multivalue TLV). The length of each item is its single-length, calculated as in Section 5.4.1 of RFC 5444. All TLVs defined in RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 have a one- or two-octet single-length, which is the expected length.

Extensions may introduce other lengths, so two principles apply:

  • If the received single-length is greater than expected, the excess octets MUST be ignored.
  • If it is less than expected, the absent octets MUST be treated as having all bits cleared (0).

There is one exception: a received CONT_SEQ_NUM with a single-length below 2 SHOULD be considered an error.
sections.eli5: If a form has extra boxes you do not know, ignore them. If it is missing boxes, pretend they are filled with zeros.

sections.title: Registries, Bit Fields and UNSPECIFIED
sections.content:
The base specifications give meanings to only some values of certain TLVs. This document turns those into IANA registries so extensions can add more. For the NHDP TLVs LOCAL_IF, LINK_STATUS and OTHER_NEIGHB, an implementation that receives any value other than those defined in RFC 6130 MUST ignore that value and the attribute association it would make for the address.

For the OLSRv2 TLVs MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE, the existing values 1, 2 and 3 are now to be read as a bit field: 1 and 2 are two separate attributes and 3 means both. A test such as Value = 1 MUST become Value bitand 1 = 1.

The three NHDP registries also gain a defined value UNSPECIFIED, meaning no information is associated with the address. It can make multivalue TLVs more efficient or simplify an implementation. For MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE the value zero already serves this purpose, and for LINK_METRIC it is possible by clearing bits 0 to 3 of the first octet. In that last case the RFC recommends that the remaining bits be all clear or all set.
sections.eli5: The messages used numbers as code words. Now the numbers are kept in a public list so people can add new code words, and there is a special "nothing to say" code word.

sections.title: The New IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA completed ten actions: five new sub-registries and five modifications to existing ones, all within the "Mobile Ad hoc NETwork (MANET) Parameters" registry. The new ones are "LOCAL_IF TLV Values", "LINK_STATUS TLV Values", "OTHER_NEIGHB TLV Values", "MPR TLV Bit Values" and "NBR_ADDR_TYPE Address Block TLV Bit Values".

In each of the three value registries, 224 to 254 are reserved for experimental use and 255 is UNSPECIFIED. The bit registries define bits 7 and 6 (values 0x01 and 0x02) and leave bits 0 to 5 unassigned. New assignments need Expert Review, and the Designated Experts must use the guidelines in RFC 6130 and RFC 7181.

For the bit registries, the experts must also preserve one sense: a set bit means the address has the property, while an unset bit means no information is provided and must not convey anything specific. In each existing "Type Extensions" sub-registry, the entry for value 0 now points to the new registry.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list book for each kind of code word. Anyone who wants to add a new one has to ask the experts who look after the book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that its changes add no new security considerations. Creating the registries, adding UNSPECIFIED (which is identical to having no TLV of that type), and reducing the latitude to reject messages all leave the base protocols' behavior unchanged. The update also introduces no opportunities for attacks through signal modification that are not already present in the two protocols.

Extensions that register TLV values in the new registries MUST specify appropriate security considerations of their own.
sections.eli5: Nothing about the new rules makes the network easier to trick. Anyone who adds new code words must explain their own safety risks.
